name: PCB

claims.claim_text: Low-cost board services removed cost as a reason not to make a custom board, leaving only the week or two of turnaround time as the argument for building a circuit any other way.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only reason not to do it is time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Bare boards are a commodity purchase, which is why in-house fabrication is now rare: milling only isolates traces from the surrounding sea of copper, leaving large areas that short easily, and aligning drills and forming vias remains the hard part.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're basically just isolating traces from the rest of the sea of copper
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Etching boards at home also imposes a chemical disposal problem that a paid service absorbs, which is a practical argument against doing it independent of quality.
claims.quote_verbatim: why would I want to be trying to figure out if I can pour copper sulfide down the drain
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Magnets, China & IEEE - Xenomorphic Xerox Xebec

claims.claim_text: The online upload-and-checkout model replaced emailing Gerbers, waiting for a quote and paying manually; the market formed around boards rather than other custom parts because every design needs a board.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone needs a custom PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Cheap board pricing comes from sharing a panel between customers, which low-cost fabricators do without telling the customer; a service that shares panels openly lets a design on the most common stack-up move through the queue faster.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the cheap PCB factories in China, they board share, but you don't know it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it

claims.claim_text: Keeping boards to a standard size makes vendor pricing comparable, so the cost effect of each option can be seen; a finish such as ENIG buys flatness and quality but can triple the price, while solder mask colour is usually free.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you keep your board to a standardized size
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For small boards the cost is dominated by tooling rather than area: a hundred small flexible boards cost seventy-seven dollars, and ordering ten instead of a hundred saves nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no difference between ordering 10 and ordering a hundred
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A fabricator's panel option means the fabricator decides the panel layout, which is usually not what the customer wants, since control over how the boards are arranged and separated belongs with the designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: their panel option means they do the panelization
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Board fabrication is specified rather than selected from a menu: material, impedance and dielectric constant can all be stated and the fabricator will attempt whatever is asked, but there are few settled standards and the manufacturer knows its own process better than an occasional customer does.
claims.quote_verbatim: You specify everything. And they will do your bidding
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Scripted output generation fails silently: a four-layer board was exported with only two layers because the output job was misconfigured, and the fault surfaced only when the fabricator's upload preview disagreed with the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: he screwed up his out job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Fabricators' preview tools also reject some legitimate output: inner plane layers exported as negative images did not render, which is a class of problem found at upload rather than at design time.
claims.quote_verbatim: doesn't like the inverse inner copper layers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Fabricators modify the customer's files as part of their process, adding rails and tooling features, and that editing step can corrupt data: a via lost information and was placed on the wrong layer, producing a short that the designer never drew.
claims.quote_verbatim: Board files were being modified by the manufacturer to add rails
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The purpose of a board is to execute the schematic faithfully, so the ideal board would have traces of zero length with no resistance, inductance or capacitance; every real board is an approximation of the schematic, and layout quality is measured by how close that approximation gets.
claims.quote_verbatim: The job of a PCB is to faithfully execute the schematic
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: An automated layout tool's obligation is to know and state its own limits, warning the user when a design exceeds what the tool has been proven to handle rather than silently producing a result.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that's, that's kind of something we already do is we, we kind of state our limitations upfront
claims.speaker: Sergiy Nesterenko

claims.claim_text: Fine-pitch packages come with an assumed process: a package specified for high-density interconnect needs via-in-pad with 0.2-millimetre vias on a 0.1-millimetre drill, filled and plated, which puts prototype cost into the thousands and forces designers to work around the recommendation when the package is the only one that fits the form factor.
claims.quote_verbatim: the official recommendation is to use via in pad
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Where a package's important pins sit deep inside the footprint, one workaround is to route over the unused pads and cover them with solder mask, which trades unused input-output for access to the pins that matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just routed over other pads
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Layer count multiplies board cost, so a twelve-layer design pushes the team to conserve area, and everyone wants the board as small as possible for that reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a 12-layer board, which makes it way more expensive
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Swapping FPGA pin assignments so signals emerge near where they must go is what keeps layer count down; without that freedom a twelve-layer board becomes the realistic option.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's pretty essential for getting the board layers down
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: Test fixtures impose mechanical load: each pogo pin exerts tens to hundreds of grams of force, so a fixture with a couple of hundred pins presses hard enough to crack the board or micro-crack multilayer ceramic capacitors if the jig is not designed to support it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Each pogo pin is, you know, tens or hundreds of grams of force
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Return of the Trade Show Jedi

claims.claim_text: Such fixtures can be bought cheaply without a formal data package: a shop that makes pogo-pin fixtures will build one from the physical board with the required holes marked in red pen, and asks for no Gerbers.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just take a red marker and you highlight all the holes that you want the Poga pins to hit
claims.speaker: Akiba

claims.claim_text: Tin whiskers grow out of a perfect solder joint over time and bend across to the adjacent pin, producing shorts that are not a workmanship defect and cannot be inspected out at build time.
claims.quote_verbatim: the tin grows and the, you know, the, they grow in these shafts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A design that works at a hundred units may fail at a hundred thousand, because a small build draws all its components from one reel while a large build spans many: parameters such as transistor threshold voltage shift across reels and across second sources, and a good design is insensitive to that spread while a marginal one stops working when an unlucky reel arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's another altogether to make a design that works even though all of the components are varying across all of their production
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: In volume production a defect compounds by the hour, because the line keeps producing the same fault while the fix is being worked out, which is why responsiveness matters more than it does at prototype scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you find a bug, every day matters. Every hour matters
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: During a component shortage the working rule became not to order boards until the parts for them are physically in hand, because availability at the time of design is no guarantee of availability at assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: do not send out a PCB until you have all the parts in your hand
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Prototype discipline varies widely: some designers will not build anything short of a final-quality board and bill of materials even for a one-off, and there is a real step in rigour between a first prototype and a run of a hundred.
claims.quote_verbatim: nothing less than an absolutely perfect final PCB and BOM is good enough for a prototype
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The sequencing rule for a new product is to get the board working on its own before it is put into a case, in the same way a constrained build gets the minimum path working before anything is bolted on.
claims.quote_verbatim: get the board working by itself before you start trying to shove it into a case
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Splitting a system across several boards joined by connectors is often driven by schedule rather than engineering: a front-end board can be finished and demonstrated at a design review while the rest is still in progress, and only sometimes is the split forced by the maximum board size.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got milestones to meet
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Once a prototype assembled from development boards has to be built in quantity, putting everything on one board and resolving the connectors is far easier than replicating a stack of modules and cabling for every unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be much easier to stick everything on one PCB and sort out all the connectors
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A middle path keeps off-the-shelf sensor breakouts but replaces the point-to-point wiring between them with a simple custom board carrying only headers, so that a five-board order is the entire production run for a demonstration unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: making it simple to solder them together in what I call like Lego prototyping
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Products are frequently the evaluation boards condensed onto one custom board, and the decision to design a part in directly rather than buy a module is made on volume and on wanting to omit what the module includes, such as its own microcontroller between the radio and the host.
claims.quote_verbatim: the final product is really just those eval boards smashed together onto a custom PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An electronics designer left to define the mechanics will produce a rectangular board with sharp corners, convenient dimensions and generous spacing; in consumer products the industrial design is fixed first and the board is shaped to it, which is a different discipline from optimising for layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to be a square board with really sharp corners
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Mechanical modelling has become part of the electronics job, because a three-dimensional model of the board is what proves it fits the enclosure; parametric modelling makes that relationship formulaic, linking board dimensions to other components rather than fixing them by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to get a 3D model of your circuit board in there to make sure it'll fit in this case
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: The two quantities that electrical and mechanical design tools have historically had to keep synchronised are the board outline and the component positions.
claims.quote_verbatim: the two things historically that we cared about were board shape and component positions

claims.claim_text: Standard board thickness is 1.6 millimetres, which is why card guides and separators are made to that width.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a standard PCB thickness that fits in vertical
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A standard board process gives the designer about five visual materials to work with: bare substrate, copper, solder mask, silkscreen and the surface finish, which is the whole palette available for decorative work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've only got four colors in quote marks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Backlighting through the board is done by clearing copper through the whole stack so a rear-mounted LED shines through the substrate, while a thin ring of copper is left around the shape and plated so the illuminated icon has a defined edge; the appearance differs between an ENIG and a hot-air-levelled finish.
claims.quote_verbatim: removed all the copper all the way through the board and then put a back under mount LED that fires through the substrate
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Exposed-copper artwork can be made electrically useful by placing a via into each exposed area and relieving the solder mask only on the opposite side, which turns a decorative pattern into a grid of contact points.
claims.quote_verbatim: I took a via and I put a via between each of the squiggles
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Inductors, transformers and antennas can be formed from copper traces on the board itself, and because the copper is being etched anyway they cost nothing but area.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've done all three of those on PCBs just with tracers and they come for free
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A heating element can be an inner-layer copper trace routed as a zigzag and brought out to high-current tabs, with the resistance and target temperature calculated in advance so the board is not delaminated by its own heater.
claims.quote_verbatim: he made a PCB with a heating element on the inner layers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Internal layers can also serve as the windings of a magnetic component, with a ferrite passing through the board and the coils formed in copper, which buys a very low-profile part.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses the internal layers to make the coils
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Standard epoxy-glass laminate has reached its frequency ceiling, which is the limit that ended a long run of using ordinary board material for ever-faster designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've come to the limit of using standard epoxy glass printed circuit boards
claims.speaker: Henry Ott
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Printed conductive traces on fabric and other flexible substrates have resistance measured in ohms per inch, which restricts them to sensing and low-current signals rather than power; printing rigid boards with the same technology is not worth doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: these are higher impedance traces
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Printing circuits onto contoured plastic competes with simply ordering a flexible board, which is already copper on plastic, so the case for the printed process rests on the geometry rather than on the conductor.
claims.quote_verbatim: why when you can just order a flex PCB, which is copper on plastic
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Machines that deposit circuit traces produce a real board rather than a printed chip, and the result is not a replacement for a fabricated board.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a replacement for a PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The board is one stage of a size hierarchy that spans six orders of magnitude: a fourteen-nanometre transistor connects to a seventy-micron die pad, then to a package trace, then to a half-millimetre BGA pitch, then to an eight-mil board trace, and the whole ladder is climbed again on the other side of the link.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going from a 14 nanometer transistor to a 70 micron die pad
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Packaging several dies into one module removes intermediate steps in that hierarchy, and the direction of travel is towards connecting dies to each other directly rather than through balls, packages and board traces; the offsetting loss is the ability to swap parts, since chip design remains far less accessible than board design.
claims.quote_verbatim: we stop putting solder balls on these things
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Chiplet integration and board integration solve the same problem at different scales: a board glues silicon to silicon through packages, bond wires and layers of laminate with all of the associated capacitance and inductance, and the primary advantage of doing it in a package instead is miniaturisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: the primary advantage is going to be miniaturization

claims.claim_text: Making the placement cost of each part visible changes design decisions: at three dollars thirty to place a forty-four-pin package, a designer can knowingly trade a little extra board area against assembly cost, and a house part that is cheaper at low volume may be dearer than a specified part at a thousand units.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's $3.30 to actually place that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Designing to a cost target can be run backwards from distributor pricing: choosing a one-cent regulator, a one-cent amplifier and a three-cent microcontroller leaves the remainder of a one-dollar budget for the board itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: That leaves me 80 cents for my PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Hardware economics differ from software in shape: an initial tooling investment is followed by a substantial per-unit cost of parts and board, which fixes the margin regardless of how many units are sold.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have an initial investment for tooling and then you have a pretty significant capital cost per unit
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: Open source hardware requires releasing the board and schematic files, not only the software; publishing the code alone does not meet the definition.
claims.quote_verbatim: You must give away your PCB and schematic files
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For an openly published design the only real protection is a trademark on the name, because the board itself, and everything on it, can be copied lawfully.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can copy your PCB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Open Hardware and The Creative Economy

claims.claim_text: A bare board is far easier to clone at high quality than a complete product with its plastics and custom connectors, so mechanical complexity is a practical deterrent to copying where legal protection is not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's easier to clone just a bare board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: Electronics magazines once printed the copper artwork at one-to-one so readers could etch their own boards, and some authors deliberately withheld it to remain the sole source of the board or the programmed part, which is an old form of the same decision open hardware makes today.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would publish the overlay for the printed circuit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Prototype boards at the technology level of a previous-generation mobile phone now cost a couple of hundred dollars delivered, and the low-cost pooling services that opened that ecosystem were followed by competitors who priced it lower still.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can now get what was like previous generation mobile phone technology, um, PCBs for, you know, uh, less than a couple of hundred dollars
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Consumer boards have become progressively harder to attack physically: vendors stopped marking debug test points, then disabled the interfaces, and the direction is towards boards carrying one or two highly integrated devices with no accessible test points, which pushes hardware attacks down to the silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: vendors have stopped obviously marking JTAG and UART test points

claims.claim_text: Reverse engineering from the board itself only works while the board is simple: a single-layer or two-layer board can be traced by eye, and a multilayer board cannot, which is why published reverse-engineered schematics of popular devices are valuable.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can look at the PCB and you know where the trace goes
claims.speaker: Michal Zalewski
claims.episode_title: The Secret Life of Circuits with lcamtuf / Michał Zalewski

claims.claim_text: Used silicon reaches the market as fragments of board: sellers cut chunks out of scrapped equipment with the expensive chip still attached, leaving the buyer to remove and reball it.
claims.quote_verbatim: on eBay, you can buy chips on PCB
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: A design tool vendor once pursued a vision in which nobody would lay out a custom board again, with pre-laid-out functional modules dropped into a design; the flagship development board was sold at four thousand dollars with the FPGA and software tooling bundled and the board layout tool deliberately excluded.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could plug these modules into your product. You would never have to design a custom PCB again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The argument for modular electronics is that a switching power supply has been laid out a million times and should be reused as a block rather than redrawn, and the argument against is that in practice a real product's constraints rarely let a fixed module drop in unchanged.
claims.quote_verbatim: Why redo the layout for a switching power supply when you can simply take it, that module and drop it in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Renders of boards read as artificial precisely because the model is too perfect; adding surface imperfections such as smudges, dust and scratches, and placing the board against a dark background, is what makes an image look like a real object.
claims.quote_verbatim: i always like to add something what i call surface imperfections
claims.speaker: Sam Aldhaher
claims.episode_title: Making The Invisible, Visible with Sam Aldhaher

claims.claim_text: Assembly animations of components falling into place on a board are scripted rather than posed by hand, which is what makes them repeatable when the design changes.
claims.quote_verbatim: i'm actually programming it all
claims.speaker: Sam Aldhaher
claims.episode_title: Making The Invisible, Visible with Sam Aldhaher

claims.claim_text: Taking a published open hardware project from its repository through fabrication, assembly, testing and driver installation is a substantial exercise in its own right, and the failures encountered along the way are where most of the learning is.
claims.quote_verbatim: How do you take, how do you go into the GitHub, take the PCB and schematic and the bomb and everything and actually get it manufactured
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A board can be designed as a prototyping substrate rather than a product, carrying a repeating grid of vias so that placement equipment has something to build onto without a project-specific layout.
claims.quote_verbatim: the board itself is made to, as, like, a template for stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Board design remains a craft learned by accumulating examples rather than from a single authority: there is no one correct layout and no definitive text, so practitioners build a mental library of patterns from reviewing other people's boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no one textbook
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

attribution_notes: ep 181, 346, 471, 593, 703: speaker labels flagged unreliable; those claims are attributed by content (an FPGA board vendor, a hardware security trainer, an EDA vendor, a former tool-vendor engineer and an open-silicon programme) and carry no name unless the identity is itself the content.
Passages with no resolved episode number were excluded entirely, including a discussion of enclosure-versus-board size conflicts.
Material about how impressive or satisfying a finished board looks was discarded as reception content.
